analysis.one_liner: Reinstates expired taxes on oil, chemical, and corporate polluters to fund toxic-waste cleanup.
analysis.headline: The bill to reinstate the Superfund taxes that expired in 1995 picked up 34 Democratic cosponsors but never got a hearing or a vote, dying in the House Ways and Means Committee at the end of the 111th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The Superfund program cleans up the nation's worst toxic-waste sites. From 1980 to 1995 it was funded mainly by taxes on the oil and chemical companies whose pollution created those sites. Those taxes expired at the end of 1995, and since then general taxpayers — not the polluting industries — have carried most of the cleanup bill. This bill would have turned the taxes back on through the end of 2017: an excise tax on crude oil and petroleum products and a corporate environmental income tax, with the money dedicated to Superfund. It was sent to the tax-writing Ways and Means Committee and never came back out.
analysis.who_benefits: Communities living near the more than 1,300 toxic-waste sites on the Superfund list, and taxpayers generally, since cleanup costs would be financed by the oil, chemical, and other corporations whose pollution created the hazard rather than by general federal revenue.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers and communities near toxic sites

how_it_helps.text: It reinstates the Hazardous Substance Superfund financing rate — an excise tax on crude oil and petroleum products — through the end of 2017.
It also reinstates the corporate environmental income tax, an income-tax surcharge on large corporations, for the same period.
The bill closes a loophole so the crude oil tax cannot be avoided by claiming an export, effective as soon as the bill is enacted.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and petrochemical companies through the crude-oil excise tax, chemical and other large corporations through the corporate environmental income tax; companies could pass some of the excise tax to consumers in fuel and product prices.

drawbacks.text: The excise tax applies to crude oil and petroleum products, so companies could pass part of it on to consumers through prices at the pump and in petroleum-based goods, meaning ordinary people would shoulder some of the cost.
The corporate environmental income tax falls on large corporations broadly, which businesses argue raises costs that can reduce investment or be shifted to customers.
Restoring the funding stream does not by itself speed up cleanup of any particular toxic site; cleanup pace depends on EPA program decisions, not just on where the money comes from.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit is real and broad: Superfund cleanups are paid for either by the companies that created the hazards or by everyone's taxes, and this bill puts that cost back on polluters, where it sat before 1996. The main costs are that part of the excise tax would likely reach consumers through fuel and chemical prices, and restoring the taxes does not itself guarantee that any particular cleanup gets done faster. On balance the design is straightforward and the burden falls mainly on the industries responsible for the sites.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Ways and Means Committee the same day, and the committee never took it up, so it expired when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Earl Blumenauer introduced the bill on January 15, 2009, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means that day.

The bill would have restored the Superfund financing rate on crude oil and petroleum products and the corporate environmental income tax, both of which had expired at the end of 1995, applying them through the end of 2017.
No committee markup, hearing, or floor vote ever appears in the action history — the record shows only the introduction, introductory remarks, and the committee referral.
Thirty-four House Democrats signed on as cosponsors over the life of the bill; no Republican did.
The bill received no further action before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011, and all House bills not passed die at that point.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The oil, petrochemical, and chemical companies that would have paid the reinstated taxes came out ahead: toxic-site cleanup costs stayed on general taxpayers instead of shifting back to the polluting industries, as the bill would have required.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and chemical companies; cleanup stayed on taxpayers

for.name: Rep. Earl Blumenauer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to reinstate the Superfund excise tax and corporate environmental income tax through 2017.

for.name: Rep. Frank Pallone
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original co-introducer of the bill.

against.name: Rep. Charles Rangel
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee the bill was referred to; the committee took no action on it — no markup, no hearing record, no vote — leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Petroleum and chemical industry lobbying
against.what_they_did: Industry groups have long opposed reinstating the Superfund taxes, which lapsed in 1995 after sustained industry opposition, and Congress declined to revive them throughout this period.

sides.party_line_note: All 34 cosponsors were Democrats and none were Republicans, but no vote ever occurred, so the partisan split was never tested on the floor.

industries.note: The bill reinstates an excise tax on crude oil and petroleum products that these companies paid until 1995. Since the tax lapsed, cleanup of toxic waste sites has been funded largely by general taxpayers instead; this bill shifts that cost back onto the industry.

industries.industry: Chemical manufacturers and large corporations generally
industries.note: The corporate environmental income tax is a surcharge on corporate income, and the Superfund financing rate touches chemical feedstocks, so chemical makers and large profitable corporations would pay more. Their gain from the bill's death was continued taxpayer funding of pollution cleanup.

Ordinary taxpayers have effectively been footing Superfund cleanup bills since the taxes expired; the bill would have relieved them of that share, though some of the excise tax could reappear in fuel and product prices.
